text: A column can look like numbers and still be text. That's one of the most common cleaning problems, because pandas only does math on numbers and only does date logic on real dates. In this lesson you'll learn to spot wrong data types and convert them safely.

Start with dtypes, or info for a fuller view. In our raw orders table every column says object, which is pandas for text. That includes the amount column, with dollar signs and commas, and the order date column. If you tried to sum amount now, you'd get string concatenation or an error, not a total.

Calling astype float directly fails: could not convert string to float, dollar sign one comma two hundred. So clean the text first, removing the dollar sign and comma with str replace. Then use to numeric with errors set to coerce. Values that can't be parsed, like n slash a, become NaN instead of crashing, and you can then handle them as missing data.

Dates work the same way. To datetime turns text into a real date column, and errors coerce turns junk like 'not recorded' into NaT, the date version of NaN. Once it's a datetime, you can filter by range, extract the month, and subtract dates, all of which you saw in the dates lesson.

Watch out for ambiguous formats. The text 03 slash 05 slash 2024 is March fifth in the United States and the third of May elsewhere. Pandas won't warn you. Parsed with a day-first format, it silently returns May third. Always pass the format argument when you know it.

Finish with the small conversions. Map yes and no text to real booleans. Convert ids stored as text with astype int. And turn a column with a few repeated labels, like tier, into a category, which is more compact and states your intent. Then check dtypes one more time.
